Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) has an established role in the preoperative staging of gastric cancer. Our prospective study confirmed that MRI is a valuable tool in conjunction with Endoscopic Ultrasonography (EUS) and Multidetector Computed Tomography (MDCT) for the accurate localization and characterization of tumor extent.

While MRI provides excellent soft-tissue contrast, particularly in cases of mesorectal invasion or suspicious nodal metastases, it does not significantly contribute to the preoperative staging of gastric cancer. EUS and MDCT have become the gold standard imaging modalities for this purpose due to their high spatial resolution, depth penetration, and ability to detect even small lymph nodes.

In our study, MRI was found to be highly sensitive in detecting occult lesions at the articular surface but limited in its ability to depict subchondral bone involvement. In contrast, EUS is excellent at visualizing the entire mesorectum, including the retroperitoneal fat and adjacent structures.

While MRI can provide additional information on lymph node status, its accuracy is often compromised due to factors such as motion artifacts, partial volume effects, and the fact that it cannot directly visualize the subchondral bone. As a result, we do not recommend routine use of MRI for preoperative staging of gastric cancer.

In conclusion, while MRI can be useful in certain contexts, EUS and MDCT remain the most reliable imaging modalities for preoperative staging of gastric cancer. However, it is essential to consider the limitations and advantages of each modality when making informed decisions about patient care.
